claims.text: Introducing a small, controlled amount of titanium into boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Titanium can be incorporated into the boride matrix during processing or through surface modification.
Titanium addition can modify the material's interfacial chemistry or microstructure.
The titanium modification will remain effective during high-temperature exposure to molten aluminum under typical hot-dip-plating times and thermal conditions.
Titanium modification will form a Ti-enriched interfacial layer or a modified boride microstructure.
The Ti-enriched layer or modified boride microstructure will resist aluminum penetration.
Titanium will segregate to grain boundaries or surfaces during processing.
Titanium segregation will produce a thin, stable titanium-containing phase or interfacial layer.
The titanium-containing phase or layer will inhibit aluminum diffusion.
The titanium-containing phase or layer will inhibit direct chemical reaction between molten aluminum and the boride phase.
Inhibiting aluminum diffusion and direct reaction will reduce corrosion kinetics relative to undoped boride.
Titanium-doped boride components will show less weight loss or pit formation than undoped controls under identical molten-aluminum exposure.
Keeping titanium content sufficiently low will preserve the integrity of the boride phase.
Deleterious titanium-associated secondary phases could compromise mechanical properties.
